content: The Enterobacteriaceae family is a large group of bacteria that includes many well-known pathogens, such as Salmonella and Escherichia coli. Genetic studies classify them within the Proteobacteria phylum, and they are assigned their own order, Enterobacteriales, although this order sometimes includes related environmental samples. Members of the Enterobacteriaceae family are rod-shaped bacteria, typically measuring 1 to 5 micrometers in length. Like other Proteobacteria, they are Gram-negative and facultative anaerobes, meaning they can survive in both oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor environments. They ferment sugars to produce lactic acid and various other end products. Additionally, they are capable of reducing nitrate to nitrite. Most members of this family are motile, possessing multiple flagella that allow them to move, although a few genera are non-motile. They do not form spores, and with the exception of Shigella dysenteriae strains, they are catalase-positive. Many Enterobacteriaceae are a normal part of the gut flora in the intestines of humans and other animals. However, some members of this family are found in water or soil, while others act as parasites on a variety of animals and plants. Escherichia coli, commonly referred to as E. coli, is one of the most important model organisms in scientific research. Its genetics and biochemistry have been extensively studied. Most Enterobacteriaceae possess peritrichous Type I fimbriae, which play a critical role in the adhesion of bacterial cells to their hosts.
